newsitem.title: FRANCE: France hails Yeltsin NATO optimism, still problems.
newsitem.headline: France hails Yeltsin NATO optimism, still problems.

text.p: France on Friday welcomed Russian President Boris Yeltsin's optimism that Moscow will reach a deal on a new relationship with NATO but said that problems remained before a planned signing of an accord in Paris on May 27.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said Yeltsin's remarks during a trip to Germany on Thursday were "confirmation of the Russian willingness to agree a planned Russia-NATO charter".
"Negotiations are continuing actively and we hope that a reasonable compromise will be quickly reached," he said.
"The staging of a summit in Paris at the end of May to sign such a charter will naturally depend on the success of the negotiations under way," he told a routine briefing.

Yeltsin, visiting German Chancellor Helmut Kohl in Baden-Baden, said: "We want to announce...that on May 27 in Paris the agreement will be signed by the leaders of the NATO countries and of Russia...So we need to hurry."
Russia's demands that NATO agree to limit the stationing of foreign troops in east European countries that join the alliance have held up preparations for the planned May 27 summit.
NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana said on Wednesday the talks were going in the right directions but might not be completed in time for the Paris meeting.

Former French Socialist prime minister Michel Rocard urged caution on NATO expansion, saying that any eastwards enlargement without a true security pact with Russia could further discourage Russia's parliament from signing disarmament treaties.
NATO is expected to invite the first east European states to join at a summit in Madrid in July despite Russian opposition. Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are favourites.

"There is still time to go back on what has been badly started, and to return to the essential: a true security treaty with Russia from which one could deduce security conditions for other European countries," Rocard wrote in the daily Le Monde.
